title: Jorinde und Joringel
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 69. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original scans). 1857 spelling preserved (daß, gieng/giengen, fieng, Thüre, Thor, Thal, todtbang, ward).
about: KHM 69, and unusual among the tales in having a known author behind it: the Grimms took it almost word for word out of Jung-Stilling’s autobiography Heinrich Stillings Jugend (1777), and its texture shows it — short abrupt sentences, descriptions that drop their verbs, very little of the usual storyteller’s furniture. A sorceress in a forest castle turns maidens into birds and keeps seven thousand of them in baskets in one room; Joringel, held motionless a hundred paces off, must find a blood-red flower before he can get Jorinde back. Spelling follows the 1857 edition, so you will meet older forms such as gieng, fieng, roth, Thal, Kreiß and todtbang.

sentences.t: Es war einmal ein altes Schloß mitten in einem großen dicken Wald, darinnen wohnte eine alte Frau ganz allein, das war eine Erzzauberin.
sentences.l: There was once an old castle in the middle of a great thick forest; in it there lived an old woman quite alone, and that was an arch-sorceress.
sentences.i: There was once an old castle in the middle of a great dense forest, and in it lived an old woman quite alone, who was a sorceress of the first order.
sentences.n: Erz- is the intensifying prefix English has as arch- (archbishop, arch-enemy); an Erzzauberin is a witch of the highest rank. dick of a wood means dense, not fat.

sentences.t: Am Tage machte sie sich zur Katze oder zur Nachteule, des Abends aber wurde sie wieder ordentlich wie ein Mensch gestaltet.
sentences.l: By day she made herself into a cat or into a night-owl, but of an evening she was formed properly again like a human being.
sentences.i: By day she made herself a cat or a night-owl, but towards evening she took proper human shape again.
sentences.n: des Abends is the genitive used adverbially for habitual time — of an evening, every evening.

sentences.t: Sie konnte das Wild und die Vögel herbei locken, und dann schlachtete sie, kochte und briet es.
sentences.l: She could lure the game and the birds to her, and then she slaughtered, boiled and roasted it.
sentences.i: She could call the game and the birds to her, and then she would slaughter them, and boil them and roast them.
sentences.n: herbei locken, two words in 1857, has herbei for motion toward the speaker — she lures them to her. The verbs that follow take a singular es, gathering game and birds into one “it”.

sentences.t: Wenn Jemand auf hundert Schritte dem Schloß nahe kam, so mußte er stille stehen und konnte sich nicht von der Stelle bewegen, bis sie ihn los sprach:
sentences.l: If anyone came near the castle within a hundred paces, then he had to stand still and could not move himself from the spot until she spoke him free:
sentences.i: If anyone came within a hundred paces of the castle, he had to stand still and could not stir from the spot until she released him with a word:
sentences.n: jemanden lossprechen — to speak someone loose, to absolve or release; the same verb is used of a priest granting absolution. The spell here is undone by speech, which is why the incantation later matters so much.

sentences.t: wenn aber eine keusche Jungfrau in diesen Kreiß kam, so verwandelte sie dieselbe in einen Vogel, und sperrte sie dann in einen Korb ein, und trug den Korb in eine Kammer des Schlosses.
sentences.l: but if a chaste maiden came into this circle, then she transformed her into a bird, and shut her then into a basket, and carried the basket into a chamber of the castle.
sentences.i: but if a chaste maiden came inside that circle, she changed her into a bird, and shut her up in a basket, and carried the basket into a chamber of the castle.
sentences.n: Kreiß is the 1857 spelling of Kreis, the circle of a hundred paces just described. dieselbe (“the same one”) is the older written language’s way of avoiding a second sie in a sentence that already has one.

sentences.t: Sie hatte wohl sieben tausend solcher Körbe mit so raren Vögeln im Schlosse.
sentences.l: She had a good seven thousand such baskets with such rare birds in the castle.
sentences.n: wohl here is not “well” but a hedge of quantity, “fully, a good.” rar means rare in the sense of choice, precious.

sentences.t: Nun war einmal eine Jungfrau, die hieß Jorinde: sie war schöner als alle andere Mädchen.
sentences.l: Now there was once a maiden who was called Jorinde: she was more beautiful than all other girls.
sentences.n: “die hieß Jorinde”: the relative pronoun begins a fresh main clause, verb second — the loose join this collection uses throughout. “alle andere Mädchen” keeps the older uninflected andere.

sentences.t: Die, und dann ein gar schöner Jüngling, Namens Joringel, hatten sich zusammen versprochen.
sentences.l: She, and then a very handsome youth by the name of Joringel, had promised themselves together.
sentences.i: She and a very handsome young man named Joringel had promised themselves to each other.
sentences.n: sich versprechen here is to become betrothed, literally to promise oneself away. Namens is a bare genitive doing the work of “by name of.”

sentences.t: Sie waren in den Brauttagen und sie hatten ihr größtes Vergnügen eins am andern.
sentences.l: They were in their bride-days, and they had their greatest pleasure one in the other.
sentences.i: They were in the days of their betrothal, and each took the greatest pleasure in the other.
sentences.n: Brauttage — the span between betrothal and wedding, when the pair were already Braut and Bräutigam but not yet married.

sentences.t: Damit sie nun einsmalen vertraut zusammen reden könnten, giengen sie in den Wald spazieren.
sentences.l: So that they might for once talk intimately together, they went walking in the forest.
sentences.i: So that for once they might talk together in confidence, they went out walking in the forest.
sentences.n: einsmalen is an old einmal, “on one occasion, for once.”

sentences.t: „Hüte dich,“ sagte Joringel, „daß du nicht so nahe ans Schloß kommst.“
sentences.l: “Take care of yourself,” said Joringel, “that you do not come so near to the castle.”
sentences.n: “sich hüten, daß … nicht” = to take care that one does not; the reflexive dich is required and the daß-clause carries its own nicht. ans = an das.

sentences.t: Es war ein schöner Abend, die Sonne schien zwischen den Stämmen der Bäume hell ins dunkle Grün des Waldes, und die Turteltaube sang kläglich auf den alten Maibuchen.
sentences.l: It was a beautiful evening, the sun shone between the trunks of the trees brightly into the dark green of the forest, and the turtle-dove sang plaintively on the old May-beeches.
sentences.i: It was a lovely evening; the sun shone between the trunks of the trees, bright in the dark green of the wood, and the turtle-dove sang mournfully in the old beeches.
sentences.n: Maibuche is a beech in its May leaf. The turtle-dove is the bird of lovers and of lament at once, and it is put here on purpose: the song that follows is about a Täubelein, a little dove.

sentences.t: Jorinde weinte zuweilen, setzte sich hin im Sonnenschein und klagte; Joringel klagte auch.
sentences.l: Jorinde wept now and then, sat herself down in the sunshine and lamented; Joringel lamented too.
sentences.n: zuweilen is the older word for now and then (modern manchmal). klagen is heavier than complaining: it is lamenting, the word used of formal mourning.

sentences.t: Sie waren so bestürzt, als wenn sie hätten sterben sollen: sie sahen sich um, waren irre und wußten nicht wohin sie nach Hause gehen sollten.
sentences.l: They were as dismayed as if they were to die: they looked around themselves, were astray and did not know which way they should go home.
sentences.i: They were as stricken as though they were about to die; they looked about them, lost their bearings, and did not know which way home lay.
sentences.n: irre sein here is to have lost the way, to be off the track, not the modern sense of being out of one’s wits.

sentences.t: Noch halb stand die Sonne über dem Berg und halb war sie unter.
sentences.l: Still half the sun stood above the mountain and half of it was down.
sentences.i: The sun stood half above the hill and was half gone down.
sentences.n: unter here is an adverb, not a preposition, standing for untergegangen — of the sun, to be down, to have set.

sentences.t: Joringel sah durchs Gebüsch und sah die alte Mauer des Schlosses nah bei sich; er erschrack und wurde todtbang.
sentences.l: Joringel looked through the bushes and saw the old wall of the castle close by him; he took fright and grew death-afraid.
sentences.i: Joringel looked through the bushes and saw the old wall of the castle close beside him; he took fright and was frightened to death.
sentences.n: todtbang (modern todbang) — “death-anxious”; German builds intensifiers by prefixing Tod-, as English does in “dead tired.” erschrack is the 1857 spelling of erschrak.

sentences.t: Jorinde sang
sentences.l: Jorinde sang

sentences.t:
„mein Vöglein mit dem Ringlein roth
singt Leide, Leide, Leide:
es singt dem Täubelein seinen Tod,
singt Leide, Lei– zucküth, zicküth, zicküth.“
sentences.l:
“my little-bird with the little-ring red
sings sorrow, sorrow, sorrow:
it sings to the little-dove his death,
sings sorrow, sorr– zucküth, zicküth, zicküth.”
sentences.i:
“my little bird with the red ring
sings of sorrow, sorrow, sorrow:
it sings to the little dove of its death,
sings sorrow, sorr– zucküth, zicküth, zicküth.”
sentences.n: The song breaks off in the middle of the word Leide and comes out as birdsong: Jorinde is turning into a nightingale as she sings it, and the last line records the change happening. What the “little red ring” is has never been settled — a ring of feathers, or the ring of her betrothal; the tale does not say, and we have not decided for it. roth is the 1857 spelling of rot.

sentences.t: Joringel sah nach Jorinde.
sentences.l: Joringel looked toward Jorinde.

sentences.t: Jorinde war in eine Nachtigall verwandelt, die sang „zicküth, zicküth.“
sentences.l: Jorinde was transformed into a nightingale, which sang “zicküth, zicküth.”
sentences.i: Jorinde had been changed into a nightingale, and it sang “zicküth, zicküth.”

sentences.t: Eine Nachteule mit glühenden Augen flog dreimal um sie herum und schrie dreimal „schu, hu, hu, hu.“
sentences.l: A night-owl with glowing eyes flew three times around her and cried three times “schu, hu, hu, hu.”
sentences.n: “flog … um sie herum” frames the object between um and herum, the doubling German needs for all the way round. Three circuits, threefold cry: three is the shape a charm takes.

sentences.t: Joringel konnte sich nicht regen: er stand da wie ein Stein, konnte nicht weinen, nicht reden, nicht Hand noch Fuß regen.
sentences.l: Joringel could not stir himself: he stood there like a stone, could not weep, not speak, not stir hand nor foot.
sentences.i: Joringel could not stir; he stood there like a stone, and could neither weep nor speak nor move hand or foot.
sentences.n: “nicht Hand noch Fuß” uses the older correlative nicht … noch where modern German says weder … noch. sich regen = to stir; the second time the reflexive is dropped.

sentences.t: Nun war die Sonne unter: die Eule flog in einen Strauch, und gleich darauf kam eine alte krumme Frau aus diesem hervor, gelb und mager: große rothe Augen, krumme Nase, die mit der Spitze ans Kinn reichte.
sentences.l: Now the sun was down: the owl flew into a bush, and straight after that there came out of it an old crooked woman, yellow and lean: great red eyes, crooked nose whose tip reached to her chin.
sentences.i: Now the sun was down; the owl flew into a bush, and immediately afterwards an old bent woman came out of it, sallow and thin, with great red eyes and a hooked nose whose tip reached her chin.
sentences.n: The description drops its verbs and its articles — große rothe Augen, krumme Nase — as if Joringel were taking her in feature by feature. The tale does this repeatedly at moments of shock.

sentences.t: Sie murmelte, fieng die Nachtigall und trug sie auf der Hand fort.
sentences.l: She muttered, caught the nightingale and carried her away on her hand.
sentences.n: fieng is the 1857 spelling of fing, from fangen. “trug sie … fort” is fortragen, separable, the fort waiting at the end of the clause.

sentences.t: Joringel konnte nichts sagen, nicht von der Stelle kommen; die Nachtigall war fort.
sentences.l: Joringel could say nothing, could not come from the spot; the nightingale was gone.
sentences.n: “nicht von der Stelle kommen”, not an inch from the spot — the same idiom as the spell of a hundred paces at the start. fort here is an adjective: gone, away.

sentences.t: Endlich kam das Weib wieder und sagte mit dumpfer Stimme „grüß dich, Zachiel, wenns Möndel ins Körbel scheint, bind los, Zachiel, zu guter Stund.“
sentences.l: At last the woman came back and said with a hollow voice “greet you, Zachiel; when the little-moon shines into the little-basket, unbind, Zachiel, in a good hour.”
sentences.i: At last the woman came back and said in a hollow voice: “A greeting to you, Zachiel; when the moon shines into the basket, loose him, Zachiel, in a good hour.”
sentences.n: This is a spell rather than a sentence, and it is not fully transparent even in German. Zachiel is a spirit-name of the kind that circulated in charm-books; Möndel and Körbel are South German diminutives of Mond and Korb. “zu guter Stund” — at a good hour, i.e. auspiciously. Anything more precise would be invention.

sentences.t: Da wurde Joringel los.
sentences.l: Then Joringel came loose.
sentences.i: And with that Joringel was released.

sentences.t: Er fiel vor dem Weib auf die Knie und bat sie möchte ihm seine Jorinde wieder geben, aber sie sagte er sollte sie nie wieder haben, und gieng fort.
sentences.l: He fell on his knees before the woman and begged she might give him his Jorinde back, but she said he should never have her again, and went away.
sentences.i: He fell on his knees before the woman and begged her to give him back his Jorinde; but she said he should never have her again, and went away.
sentences.n: Two reported clauses with no conjunction: “bat sie möchte …”, “sie sagte er sollte …”. The subjunctives möchte and sollte do the work daß would otherwise do.

sentences.t: Er rief, er weinte, er jammerte, aber alles umsonst.
sentences.l: He called, he wept, he wailed, but all in vain.

sentences.t: „Uu, was soll mir geschehen?“
sentences.l: “Oo, what is to become of me?”
sentences.n: A cry rather than a word — the text simply prints the sound. “was soll mir geschehen” is literally “what shall happen to me,” with the person in the dative.

sentences.t: Joringel gieng fort und kam endlich in ein fremdes Dorf: da hütete er die Schafe lange Zeit.
sentences.l: Joringel went away and came at last into a strange village: there he tended the sheep a long time.
sentences.i: Joringel went away and came at last to a village where he was a stranger, and there he kept the sheep for a long while.
sentences.n: fremd is strange in the sense of not one’s own: the village is a stranger’s to him, not an odd one. hüten of animals is to keep, to watch over.

sentences.t: Oft gieng er rund um das Schloß herum, aber nicht zu nahe dabei.
sentences.l: Often he went round about the castle, but not too near to it.
sentences.n: The circling is doubled again — rund um … herum. dabei = by it, near it; German fuses the pronoun to its preposition.

sentences.t: Endlich träumte er einmal des Nachts er fände eine blutrothe Blume, in deren Mitte eine schöne große Perle war.
sentences.l: At last he dreamed one night that he found a blood-red flower, in the middle of which was a fine great pearl.
sentences.i: At last, one night, he dreamed that he found a blood-red flower with a fine great pearl in the middle of it.
sentences.n: fände is subjunctive: it holds the whole sentence inside the dream. des Nachts is the adverbial genitive again — by night.

sentences.t: Die Blume brach er ab, gieng damit zum Schlosse: alles, was er mit der Blume berührte, ward von der Zauberei frei: auch träumte er, er hätte seine Jorinde dadurch wieder bekommen.
sentences.l: The flower he broke off, went with it to the castle: everything that he touched with the flower became free of the enchantment: he dreamed too that he had got his Jorinde back by this means.
sentences.i: He broke the flower off and went with it to the castle; everything he touched with it was freed from the enchantment, and he dreamed too that by this means he had got his Jorinde back again.
sentences.n: “Die Blume brach er ab” puts the object first and the subject third: the verb holds second place and anything at all may stand before it. abbrechen is separable, its ab at the end.

sentences.t: Des Morgens, als er erwachte, fieng er an durch Berg und Thal zu suchen ob er eine solche Blume fände: er suchte bis an den neunten Tag, da fand er die blutrothe Blume am Morgen früh.
sentences.l: In the morning, when he awoke, he began to search through mountain and valley whether he might find such a flower: he searched until the ninth day, then he found the blood-red flower early in the morning.
sentences.i: In the morning, when he awoke, he began to search through hill and dale to see whether he could find such a flower; he searched until the ninth day, and then, early in the morning, he found the blood-red flower.
sentences.n: “durch Berg und Thal” is the fixed pairing English has as “over hill and dale.” Thal is the 1857 spelling of Tal.

sentences.t: In der Mitte war ein großer Thautropfe, so groß wie die schönste Perle.
sentences.l: In the middle was a great dew-drop, as big as the finest pearl.
sentences.n: The dream promised a pearl and the waking world gives a drop of dew — the tale lets the substitution stand without comment.

sentences.t: Diese Blume trug er Tag und Nacht bis zum Schloß.
sentences.l: This flower he carried day and night as far as the castle.

sentences.t: Wie er auf hundert Schritt nahe bis zum Schloß kam, da ward er nicht fest, sondern gieng fort bis ans Thor.
sentences.l: When he came within a hundred paces of the castle, then he did not become fixed, but rather went on as far as the gate.
sentences.i: When he came within a hundred paces of the castle he was not held fast, but went on as far as the gate.
sentences.n: wie here is the temporal als, “when”, common in speech and in the older written language. “ward er nicht fest” — festwerden, of the spell that fixed anyone within a hundred paces.

sentences.t: Joringel freute sich hoch, berührte die Pforte mit der Blume, und sie sprang auf.
sentences.l: Joringel rejoiced highly, touched the door with the flower, and it sprang open.
sentences.i: Joringel rejoiced greatly, touched the door with the flower, and it sprang open.
sentences.n: aufspringen, of a door, is to fly open of itself, not to spring up. Pforte and Thor stand two lines apart for the same entrance.

sentences.t: Er gieng hinein, durch den Hof, horchte wo er die vielen Vögel vernähme: endlich hörte ers.
sentences.l: He went in, through the courtyard, listened for where he might make out the many birds: at last he heard it.
sentences.i: He went in, across the courtyard, and listened for where he might catch the sound of the many birds; at last he heard it.
sentences.n: vernähme is subjunctive after an indirect question — where he might hear them, the place not yet known.

sentences.t: Er gieng und fand den Saal, darauf war die Zauberin und fütterte die Vögel in den sieben tausend Körben.
sentences.l: He went and found the hall, and in it was the sorceress and was feeding the birds in the seven thousand baskets.
sentences.i: He went on and found the hall, and there was the sorceress, feeding the birds in the seven thousand baskets.
sentences.n: darauf is locative: older German says auf dem Saal where we now say in dem Saal (compare auf der Stube, auf dem Zimmer), so darauf = in it — hung on loosely, like the opening “darinnen wohnte eine alte Frau”.

sentences.t: Wie sie den Joringel sah, ward sie bös, sehr bös, schalt, spie Gift und Galle gegen ihn aus, aber sie konnte auf zwei Schritte nicht an ihn kommen.
sentences.l: When she saw the Joringel, she grew angry, very angry, scolded, spat poison and gall out at him, but she could not come within two paces of him.
sentences.i: When she saw Joringel she grew angry, very angry, and scolded and spat poison and gall at him, but she could not come within two paces of him.
sentences.n: “Gift und Galle speien” — to spit poison and gall, the German for raging at somebody. den Joringel with the article before a personal name is colloquial and warm; it is how people are spoken of in speech rather than in books.

sentences.t: Er kehrte sich nicht an sie und gieng, besah die Körbe mit den Vögeln; da waren aber viele hundert Nachtigallen, wie sollte er nun seine Jorinde wieder finden?
sentences.l: He did not turn himself to her and went, looked over the baskets with the birds; but there were many hundreds of nightingales — how should he now find his Jorinde again?
sentences.i: He paid her no heed, but went along looking over the baskets of birds; and there were many hundreds of nightingales — how was he to find his Jorinde among them?
sentences.n: “sich an jemanden kehren” — to turn oneself to someone, i.e. to take notice of them; almost always used in the negative.

sentences.t: Indem er so zusah, daß die Alte heimlich ein Körbchen mit einem Vogel wegnahm und damit nach der Thüre gieng.
sentences.l: While he was looking on like this, [he saw] that the old woman secretly took away a little basket with a bird in it and went with it toward the door.
sentences.n: The sentence is broken as it stands: the daß-clause has no main verb to hang on, and something like er sah (“he saw”) has dropped out between them. The 1857 edition prints it this way and we leave the German untouched; the square brackets in the literal supply what the German omits. Brackets mean that throughout Lectorium — words the original does not have, added so the English can stand up.

sentences.t: Flugs sprang er hinzu, berührte das Körbchen mit der Blume und auch das alte Weib: nun konnte sie nichts mehr zaubern, und Jorinde stand da, hatte ihn um den Hals gefaßt, so schön wie sie ehemals war.
sentences.l: In a flash he sprang over, touched the little basket with the flower and the old woman too: now she could work no more magic, and Jorinde stood there, had taken him about the neck, as beautiful as she was formerly.
sentences.i: In a flash he sprang across and touched the little basket with the flower, and the old woman too; and now she could work no more magic, and there stood Jorinde with her arms about his neck, as beautiful as she had been before.
sentences.n: flugs (from Flug, flight) — in a flash, at once. The tense slips from past to pluperfect and back inside the one sentence, so that the embrace has already happened by the time we see her standing there.

sentences.t: Da machte er auch alle die andern Vögel wieder zu Jungfrauen, und da gieng er mit seiner Jorinde nach Hause, und sie lebten lange vergnügt zusammen.
sentences.l: Then he made all the other birds into maidens again too, and then he went home with his Jorinde, and they lived long and contented together.
sentences.i: Then he made all the other birds into maidens again as well, and went home with his Jorinde, and they lived long and happily together.
sentences.n: The tale does not end “ever after”: lange vergnügt is long and contented, which is a smaller and more human claim.
